name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q01 - Dispersion force between two nonpolar atoms

questiontext.text:
The diagram below shows two identical nonpolar atoms X and Y in close proximity, where a momentary distortion of the electron cloud in Atom X induces a dipole in Atom Y.

Identify the type of intermolecular force illustrated and the dependence of its interaction energy on the intermolecular distance \(r\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows two nonpolar atoms, X and Y, placed close to each other. Atom X has an asymmetrical electron cloud with partial positive (\(\delta^+\)) charge on the left and partial negative (\(\delta^-\)) charge on the right, representing an instantaneous dipole. Atom Y shows a matching induced dipole with \(\delta^+\) facing the \(\delta^-\) end of Atom X.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Nonpolar atoms have a symmetrical electronic charge distribution on average, so permanent dipoles are absent. The interaction is purely attractive between transient partial charges at short range (\(\sim 500\text{ pm}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The attractive force between an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole is called a London force or dispersion force. Its interaction energy \(E\) varies with distance \(r\) as \(E \propto \frac{1}{r^6}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because Atom X develops a temporary dipole that distorts the electron cloud of Atom Y, the resulting attraction between the two temporary dipoles is a dispersion (London) force. Unlike stationary dipole–dipole interactions (which vary as \(\frac{1}{r^3}\)), dispersion interaction energy decays inversely with the sixth power of distance, \(\frac{1}{r^6}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The interaction is always attractive and its magnitude increases with polarisability. Therefore, the illustrated interaction is a dispersion (London) force with interaction energy proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^6}\).

answer.text: Dipole–dipole force between stationary dipoles; interaction energy proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^3}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q02 - Boyles law isotherms p vs V

questiontext.text:
The graph below shows pressure \(p\) versus volume \(V\) isotherms for a fixed amount of an ideal gas at three different constant temperatures \(T_1\), \(T_2\), and \(T_3\).

Which of the following relationships between \(T_1\), \(T_2\), and \(T_3\) is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(p\) versus \(V\) plot displays three hyperbolic curves (isotherms) for a fixed amount \(n\) of an ideal gas, with the curve for \(T_1\) lying lowest, \(T_2\) in the middle, and \(T_3\) lying highest.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both \(p\) and \(V\) are positive quantities, and temperature \(T\) is measured on the absolute (Kelvin) scale.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Boyle's law and the ideal gas equation, \(pV = nRT\). At a fixed volume \(V\), pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature: \(p = \left(\frac{nR}{V}\right)T\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Consider a vertical line at any constant volume \(V_0\). Moving upward along this vertical line, the pressure increases from the \(T_1\) curve to the \(T_2\) curve and is highest on the \(T_3\) curve, so \(p_3 > p_2 > p_1\). Since \(p \propto T\) at constant \(V\) and \(n\), it follows directly that \(T_3 > T_2 > T_1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Higher isotherms on a \(p\)–\(V\) diagram correspond to larger \(pV\) values and therefore higher temperatures. Thus, \(T_3 > T_2 > T_1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q03 - Boyles law p vs 1/V slope and moles

questiontext.text:
The graph shows \(p\) versus \(\frac{1}{V}\) plots for \(n\) moles of an ideal gas at three different temperatures \(T_X\), \(T_Y\), and \(T_Z\).

Which statement correctly compares the temperatures and describes the effect of doubling the number of moles \(n\) on the slope of a line at constant temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(p\) versus \(\frac{1}{V}\) graph consists of three straight lines passing through the origin for \(n\) moles of an ideal gas. The steepest line is labelled \(T_X\), the middle line is \(T_Y\), and the shallowest line is \(T_Z\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas behaves ideally, so \(pV = nRT\) holds, and \(T_X, T_Y, T_Z\) are absolute temperatures in Kelvin.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Rewriting the ideal gas equation gives \(p = (nRT)\left(\frac{1}{V}\right)\). Comparing with \(y = mx\), the slope of the \(p\) versus \(\frac{1}{V}\) line is \(m = nRT = k_1\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(n\) and \(R\) are constant across the three lines, a steeper slope \(m = nRT\) corresponds to a higher temperature \(T\). Because the slope decreases from \(T_X\) to \(T_Y\) to \(T_Z\), we have \(T_X > T_Y > T_Z\). Furthermore, if the number of moles \(n\) is doubled while keeping \(T\) constant, the new slope becomes \(m' = (2n)RT = 2m\), so the slope doubles.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The proportionality constant \(k_1 = nRT\) depends on both temperature and amount of gas. Therefore, \(T_X > T_Y > T_Z\), and doubling \(n\) at constant temperature doubles the slope.

answer.text: \(T_Z > T_Y > T_X\), and the slope doubles when \(n\) is doubled.
\(T_X > T_Y > T_Z\), and the slope doubles when \(n\) is doubled.
\(T_X > T_Y > T_Z\), and the slope is halved when \(n\) is doubled.
\(T_Z > T_Y > T_X\), and the slope remains unchanged when \(n\) is doubled.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q04 - Charles law isobars V vs T in Celsius

questiontext.text:
The volume versus temperature (\(^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) graph for a fixed mass of an ideal gas at four different constant pressures \(p_1\), \(p_2\), \(p_3\), and \(p_4\) is shown below, with all extrapolated lines meeting at \(-273.15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Which pressure ordering is correct for the four isobars shown?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The plot shows four straight-line isobars of volume \(V\) versus Celsius temperature \(t\) for a fixed mass of gas, all intersecting the temperature axis at \(-273.15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\). The slopes decrease in the order: line \(p_1\) (steepest), \(p_2\), \(p_3\), and \(p_4\) (shallowest).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas obeys Charles' law and the ideal gas equation \(pV = nRT\), where \(T = t + 273.15\) is in Kelvin and \(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4\) are positive pressures.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From \(V = \left(\frac{nR}{p}\right)T = \left(\frac{nR}{p}\right)(t + 273.15)\), the slope of the \(V\) versus \(t\) line is \(\frac{nR}{p}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(n\) and \(R\) are fixed, the slope \(\frac{nR}{p}\) is inversely proportional to pressure \(p\). Alternatively, at any fixed temperature (such as \(0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)), \(V\) is largest on the \(p_1\) line and smallest on the \(p_4\) line (\(V_1 > V_2 > V_3 > V_4\)). By Boyle's law at constant temperature, \(p \propto \frac{1}{V}\), which gives \(p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < p_4\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Steeper isobars correspond to lower pressures. Therefore, the correct ordering is \(p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < p_4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q05 - Gay Lussacs law isochores p vs T

questiontext.text:
The pressure versus Kelvin temperature graph (isochores) for a fixed amount of an ideal gas at four constant molar volumes \(V_1\), \(V_2\), \(V_3\), and \(V_4\) is shown below.

Which relationship among the volumes \(V_1\), \(V_2\), \(V_3\), and \(V_4\) is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(p\) versus \(T\) (K) graph displays four straight lines (isochores) passing through the origin \((0,0)\) for a fixed amount of ideal gas. The slopes decrease from \(V_1\) (steepest) through \(V_2\) and \(V_3\) to \(V_4\) (shallowest).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas obeys Gay-Lussac's law and the ideal gas equation \(pV = nRT\), with \(T\) in Kelvin and \(V_1, V_2, V_3, V_4 > 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Rearranging the ideal gas equation gives \(p = \left(\frac{nR}{V}\right)T\). Thus, the slope of each \(p\)–\(T\) isochore is \(\frac{nR}{V}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(nR\) is constant, the slope \(\frac{nR}{V}\) is inversely proportional to the volume \(V\). Because the slope is greatest for \(V_1\) and smallest for \(V_4\), the volumes must increase in the reverse order: \(V_1 < V_2 < V_3 < V_4\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At a fixed temperature (say \(200\text{ K}\)), the pressure is highest for \(V_1\) and lowest for \(V_4\); by Boyle's law, higher pressure at constant temperature means smaller volume. Hence, \(V_1 < V_2 < V_3 < V_4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q06 - Maxwell Boltzmann speed markers and ratio

questiontext.text:
The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of molecular speeds for a gas at a given temperature is shown below, with three characteristic speeds marked as \(u_1\), \(u_2\), and \(u_3\).

Identify \(u_1\), \(u_2\), and \(u_3\), and select their correct ratio \(u_1 : u_2 : u_3\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution curve starts at \((0,0)\), rises to a single maximum, and tails off at high speeds. Three vertical lines mark speeds in increasing order from left to right: \(u_1\) at the peak of the curve, \(u_2\) to the right of the peak, and \(u_3\) further to the right.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas is at a fixed temperature \(T\), so the distribution of molecular speeds is stationary, and \(u_1 < u_2 < u_3\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The speed corresponding to the maximum of the distribution curve (possessed by the largest fraction of molecules) is the most probable speed \(u_{\text{mp}}\). The three characteristic speeds follow the order \(u_{\text{rms}} > u_{\text{av}} > u_{\text{mp}}\) and the ratio \(u_{\text{mp}} : u_{\text{av}} : u_{\text{rms}} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(u_1\) lies at the maximum of the curve, \(u_1 = u_{\text{mp}}\). Because \(u_{\text{mp}} < u_{\text{av}} < u_{\text{rms}}\), the intermediate marker \(u_2\) corresponds to the average speed \(u_{\text{av}}\), and the largest marker \(u_3\) corresponds to the root mean square speed \(u_{\text{rms}}\). Their ratio is \(1 : 1.128 : 1.224\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ordering \(u_{\text{mp}} < u_{\text{av}} < u_{\text{rms}}\) matches \(u_1 < u_2 < u_3\). Thus, \(u_1 = u_{\text{mp}}\), \(u_2 = u_{\text{av}}\), \(u_3 = u_{\text{rms}}\), and \(u_1 : u_2 : u_3 = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q07 - Speed distribution of chlorine and nitrogen at 300 K

questiontext.text:
The graph below shows the molecular speed distribution curves for two gases, \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), at \(300\text{ K}\), labelled Curve P and Curve Q.

Which assignment of Curve P and Curve Q is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Both curves are recorded at \(T = 300\text{ K}\). Curve P has a sharper, taller peak at a lower molecular speed, whereas Curve Q has a broader, shorter peak shifted to a higher molecular speed. The molar masses are \(M_{\mathrm{N_2}} = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{Cl_2}} = 71\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both gases are at the same temperature (\(300\text{ K}\)), so they have the same average translational kinetic energy per molecule.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
At a fixed temperature, heavier gas molecules move more slowly than lighter gas molecules, resulting in a lower most probable speed \(u_{\text{mp}}\) and a narrower speed distribution.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(M_{\mathrm{Cl_2}} > M_{\mathrm{N_2}}\), chlorine molecules move slower on average and have a lower \(u_{\text{mp}}\) than nitrogen molecules at \(300\text{ K}\). Therefore, the curve peaking at the lower speed (Curve P) represents \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), and the broader curve peaking at the higher speed (Curve Q) represents \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Lighter \(\mathrm{N_2}\) molecules have a higher most probable speed than heavier \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) molecules at \(300\text{ K}\). Hence, Curve P represents \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) and Curve Q represents \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

answer.text: Curve P represents \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and Curve Q represents \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) because heavier molecules move faster at \(300\text{ K}\).
Curve P represents \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) and Curve Q represents \(\mathrm{N_2}\) because lighter \(\mathrm{N_2}\) molecules have a higher most probable speed at \(300\text{ K}\).
Curve P represents \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and Curve Q represents \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) because \(\mathrm{N_2}\) has a narrower distribution of speeds.
Both curves could represent either gas because molecular speed depends only on temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q08 - Surface tension forces on surface and bulk molecules

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the intermolecular attractive forces acting on a molecule S at the surface of a liquid and a molecule M in the interior (bulk) of the liquid.

Which statement accurately describes the net force and energy of Molecule S compared to Molecule M?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The beaker diagram shows Molecule M deep inside the liquid surrounded symmetrically by force arrows in all directions, and Molecule S at the liquid–air interface with force arrows pointing sideways and downward into the liquid, with no molecules above it.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All arrows represent attractive intermolecular forces exerted by neighbouring liquid molecules.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By vector symmetry, equal attractive forces from all sides cancel out in the bulk, whereas an unbalanced inward attraction acts at the surface. Pulling a molecule from the bulk to the surface requires work against these attractive forces, increasing surface energy.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For Molecule M, forces in opposite directions cancel, giving zero net force. For Molecule S, there are no liquid molecules above the surface to balance the downward pull of molecules below, so Molecule S experiences a net downward force toward the interior. Because energy must be expended to bring a molecule from the interior to the surface, Molecule S has higher energy than Molecule M.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
To minimise total energy, liquids tend to have the minimum number of molecules at the surface, i.e., minimum surface area. Thus, Molecule S experiences a net downward force and has higher energy than Molecule M.

answer.text: Molecule S experiences zero net force and has lower energy than Molecule M.
Molecule S experiences a net upward force and has the same energy as Molecule M.
Molecule M experiences a net downward force and has higher energy than Molecule S.
Molecule S experiences a net downward force into the liquid and has higher energy than Molecule M.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q09 - Compressibility factor Z vs pressure for H2 and CO2

questiontext.text:
The plot below shows the variation of compressibility factor \(Z = \frac{pV}{nRT}\) with pressure \(p\) (in bar) at \(273\text{ K}\) for an ideal gas and two real gases, Curve X (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)) and Curve Y (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)).

Which interpretation of Curve X and Curve Y is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
At \(273\text{ K}\), the horizontal line at \(Z = 1\) represents an ideal gas. Curve X (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)) starts at \(Z = 1\) at \(p \to 0\) and increases linearly above \(1\) with pressure. Curve Y (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)) drops sharply below \(Z = 1\) at intermediate pressures, reaches a minimum, and then rises above \(Z = 1\) at high pressures.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(Z = \frac{V_{\text{real}}}{V_{\text{ideal}}}\). Values \(Z < 1\) indicate negative deviation (gas is more compressible than ideal), while \(Z > 1\) indicates positive deviation (gas is less compressible than ideal).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In the van der Waals equation \(\left(p + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT\), the constant \(a\) represents intermolecular attractive forces and \(b\) represents the excluded molecular volume due to short-range repulsions.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (Curve Y), \(273\text{ K}\) is below its Boyle temperature, and strong intermolecular attractions (\(a\)) pull molecules together at intermediate pressures, making \(V_{\text{real}} < V_{\text{ideal}}\) and \(Z < 1\). At very high pressures, the \(nb\) volume correction dominates and \(Z > 1\). For \(\mathrm{H_2}\) (Curve X), \(273\text{ K}\) is above its Boyle temperature; intermolecular attractions are very feeble, so the excluded volume term \(b\) and repulsive forces dominate across all positive pressures, keeping \(Z > 1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All gases approach \(Z = 1\) as \(p \to 0\). Therefore, Curve Y dips below \(Z = 1\) at intermediate pressures due to dominant intermolecular attractions (\(a\)), while Curve X remains above \(Z = 1\) because excluded volume/repulsive effects (\(b\)) dominate at \(273\text{ K}\).

answer.text: Curve Y has \(Z < 1\) at intermediate pressures because \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) molecules have negligible intermolecular attraction.

Curve Y shows \(Z < 1\) at intermediate pressures because intermolecular attractive forces (\(a\)) dominate, whereas Curve X stays at \(Z > 1\) because excluded volume effects (\(b\)) dominate at \(273\text{ K}\).
Curve X stays above \(Z = 1\) because \(\mathrm{H_2}\) has a much larger van der Waals constant \(a\) than \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).
At \(p \to 0\), both Curve X and Curve Y diverge away from \(Z = 1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q10 - Andrews isotherms of CO2 and two-phase equilibrium

questiontext.text:
The \(p\)–\(V\) isotherms of carbon dioxide obtained by Thomas Andrews are shown below, with critical point E at \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(73\text{ atm}\).

Along the \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) isotherm, what happens during isothermal compression from point B to point C?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows Andrews' \(p\)–\(V\) isotherms for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). The shaded dome encloses the two-phase region, with critical point E at \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(73\text{ atm}\). Along the \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) isotherm, compression proceeds from gas at A, reaches the dome boundary at B, follows a horizontal plateau to C, and then rises steeply toward D.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The compression is carried out isothermally at \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), which is below the critical temperature \(T_c = 30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Below \(T_c\), isothermal compression of a gas causes condensation once the saturation vapour pressure is reached. Inside the dome, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium at constant pressure.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At point B, liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) appears for the first time. As volume is reduced from B to C, the pressure remains constant while gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) continuously condenses into liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). At point C, all the gas has condensed into liquid, and further compression along the steep line toward D compresses the nearly incompressible liquid.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Along the horizontal segment between B and C, liquid and gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) coexist in equilibrium at constant pressure, with more gas condensing into liquid as volume decreases until complete liquefaction at C.

answer.text: Only gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is present, and its pressure increases linearly with decreasing volume.
Carbon dioxide behaves as a supercritical fluid with no phase boundary between liquid and gas.
Liquid and gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) coexist in equilibrium at constant pressure, and decreasing volume condenses more gas until all gas becomes liquid at C.
All \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is already liquid at B, and the segment from B to C represents expansion of the liquid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q11 - Vapour pressure vs temperature curves and boiling points

questiontext.text:
The vapour pressure versus temperature curves for three liquids L, M, and N are shown below, along with a dashed line at \(760\text{ mm Hg}\) (\(1\text{ atm}\)).

Based on the curves, which ordering of normal boiling points and intermolecular attractive forces for L, M, and N is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph plots vapour pressure (mm Hg) against temperature (K) for three liquids L, M, and N. At the dashed \(760\text{ mm Hg}\) line, Curve L intersects at \(308\text{ K}\), Curve M at \(351.3\text{ K}\), and Curve N at \(373\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The normal boiling point is defined as the temperature at which the equilibrium vapour pressure of a liquid equals \(1\text{ atm}\) (\(760\text{ mm Hg}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Stronger intermolecular attractive forces make it harder for molecules to escape into the vapour phase, resulting in a lower vapour pressure at a given temperature and a higher normal boiling point.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the \(760\text{ mm Hg}\) intersections, the normal boiling points are \(308\text{ K}\) for L, \(351.3\text{ K}\) for M, and \(373\text{ K}\) for N, giving the boiling-point order \(\text{L} < \text{M} < \text{N}\). At any fixed temperature, liquid L has the highest vapour pressure and liquid N has the lowest. Consequently, intermolecular attractive forces are weakest in L and strongest in N: \(\text{L} < \text{M} < \text{N}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Higher vapour pressure corresponds to weaker intermolecular forces and a lower normal boiling point. Therefore, both the normal boiling points and the intermolecular attractive forces increase in the order \(\text{L} < \text{M} < \text{N}\).
